system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, severe asthma, and chronic abdominal pain was admitted for an asthma exacerbation and worsening epigastric pain. He had not followed up with specialists after a recent intubation for asthma. Initial management included bronchodilators and steroids for asthma. Abdominal pain persisted despite normal CT and ultrasound; an EGD revealed candidal esophagitis and CMV-positive gastric ulcers, leading to treatment with fluconazole and valganciclovir. An MRCP showed cirrhosis and a 6.2 cm liver nodule concerning for dysplastic changes or early malignancy, necessitating outpatient hepatology follow-up for biopsy. Asthma improved with therapy, and he was discharged home on multiple new medications with plans for pulmonology, ID, and GI follow-up. He committed to sobriety and adherence to care.
problems: Gastric ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old gentleman with a history of asthma 
and multiple prior intubations for asthma exacerbation on 
chronic steroids as well as history of alcoholic cirrhosis and 
pancreatitis who presents with 3 days of rapidly worsening 
dyspnea in the setting of an alcohol binge.

ACTIVE ISSUES
-------------
# Asthma exacerbation: Has a history of recently worsening 
asthma with multiple hospital admissions and recent intubation 
at ___ and other hospitals. He was last admitted for 
exacerbation at ___ in ___. He has undergone extensive 
workup to explain recently worsening asthma, including 
Aspergillus and Strongyloides serologies, both of which were 
negative. Differential for exacerbation includes viral 
etiologies and environmental allergens. He had no evidence of 
pneumonia on CXR. On admission he received magnesium, nebulizers 
and methylprednisolone in the ED. In the ICU, he was initially 
started on methylprednisolone IV and transitioned to PO 
prednisone. He was also started on continuous nebulizer 
treatments, which were spaced out when respiratory status 
improved. He required BiPAP but never needed intubation. He was 
transferred to the floor on ___, and was continued on a 
prednisone taper, monteleukast, and alternating ipratropium and 
albuterol nebulizers. He was started on oseltamivir while in the 
ICU pending viral cultures, which was stopped when respiratory 
viral panel returned negative. ___ levels to rule out 
vasculitis were also negative. IgE levels were sent to evaluate 
his candidacy for Xolair and returned normal. The cause of his 
current and recurrent exacerbations is unknown.  At time of 
discharge his respiratory status was at baseline. He was 
discharged on a long prednisone taper (60 mg for 1 days through 
___, then 5 days 40mg, 5 days 20mg, and 5 days 10mg (finishing 
taper on ___. He was started on atovaquone for PCP 
prophylaxis while on a prednisone taper, and should stop 
atovaquone after prednisone finishes. He was also instructed to 
follow up with pulmonology and sleep medicine for PFTs/DLCO and 
a sleep study to evaluate for CPAP. He will need allergy testing 
after prednisone is completed to help clarify the cause of his 
frequent exacerbations. He should also possibly have a dedicated 
neck CT as an outpatient for assessment of 
tracheobronchomalacia.

# Alcohol intoxication: Patient has a history of alcohol abuse 
and withdrawal seizures. He has reportedly been sober for the 
past 6 months. He started drinking again 3 days prior to 
admission, drinking hard alcohol continuously, in an attempt to 
numb his respiratory symptoms and avoid coming to the ED. His 
last drink was at 1600 on the night prior to admission. ETOH 
level was 307 in the ED. He was maintained on CIWA scale and 
received diazepam for mild alcohol withdrawal. However, it was 
unclear if his withdrawal symptoms were instead related to 
anxiety from asthma and tachycardia from albuterol and he was 
quickly weaned off diazepam.

# Alcoholic cirrhosis: Has a history of alcoholic cirrhosis 
complicated by thrombocytopenia. He takes nadolol, 
spironolactone, lasix at home. MRCP on prior admission was 
notable for T1 hyperintense, subtly arterially enhancing nodules 
within the right hepatic lobe, spanning an area of up to 6.2 x 
2.3 cm in the axial plane. While admitted, furosemide and 
spironolactone were continued. Nadolol was held in the setting 
of asthma exacerbation. He will need outpatient follow up with 
Dr. ___ repeat imaging of liver within the next 2 months. 
Nadolol was held at discharge and he was instructed to follow up 
with his PCP regarding when to restart.

# Immunodeficiency/CMV gastritis: Secondary to chronic steroid 
use resulting in CMV gastritis and ___ esophagitis. 
Valgancyclovir was started on ___ at an induction dose of 900mg 
Q12 though patient had not been taking this for the three days 
prior to admission. He noted that he completed a course of 
bactrim for PCP ___. He had a negative HIV test in the 
past year, so his CMV gastritis was attributed to his steroid 
use. We continued valgancyclovir at maintenance dose of 900mg 
Q24. He will require a 3-month maintenance course.

# Abdominal pain: he also had a flare of his chronic abdominal 
pain. Review of prior records revealed that he presented 
similarly with his CMV gastritis. He was continued on 
valgancyclovir as above. He was also treated with hydromorphone 
while in the hospital, but weaned off and will resume Suboxone 
at discharge. 

# Bilateral lower extremity edema: Likely secondary to 
cirrhosis, though last albumin in ___ was normal. 
Differential also includes venous stasis. BNP on admission was 
unremarkable. We continued spironolactone and furosemide. His 
TTE from ___ was reviewed and revealed mild right 
ventricular dilation and normal biventricular systolic function 
so edema related to right sided failure was ruled out.

# Sinus tachycardia: Likely secondary to continuous albuterol 
nebs, though there may have been a component of alcohol 
withdrawal as well. Epigastric pain also likely contributed. He 
was maintained on CIWA scale. Abdominal pain improved with 
narcotic regimen.

# Thrombocytopenia: Has baseline thrombocytopenia, likely due to 
cirrhosis. We continued to monitor and platelets remained stable

triamcinolone cream

# Immunodeficiency/CMV gastritis: Secondary to chronic steroid

# Abdominal pain: he also had a flare of his chronic abdominal

# Bilateral lower extremity edema: Likely secondary to

Differential also includes venous stasis. BNP on admission was

# Sinus tachycardia: Likely secondary to continuous albuterol

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the medical team. You're in the ICU now. You came in because you were having a lot of trouble breathing. Can you tell me how you're feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t catch my breath… even with this mask. It’s been getting worse for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. You’re on BiPAP to help support your breathing. We’ve started you on steroids and nebulizers. Your oxygen is improving. Do you remember why you waited to come in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was drinking… trying to calm down. I didn’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your alcohol level was high when you arrived. We’re monitoring you for withdrawal, but your fast heart rate is likely from both the albuterol and anxiety. We’ll keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach’s been killing me too. It’s been bad for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your exam shows tenderness in the upper abdomen. Given your history, we’re concerned it might be related to your CMV gastritis. Are you still taking your valganciclovir?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped it a few days ago. I ran out and didn’t refill it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that could explain the flare-up. We’ve restarted it at a lower dose for maintenance. We also checked for infections—your flu and other virus tests came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not the flu? Good. But why do I keep having these asthma attacks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. Your IgE level was normal, so allergies might not be the main trigger. We’re ruling out other causes. You’ve had a chest X-ray—no pneumonia. But it did show some fluid buildup in the lungs, possibly from heart strain or fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My legs are swollen too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your cirrhosis likely contributes. We checked your legs for clots—no DVT. Your heart function from a past echo was okay, so we think the swelling is from liver disease. We’re continuing your diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver? I remember something about a nodule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from your last MRCP, there’s a 6.2 cm nodule in your liver. It’s concerning. You need follow-up with hepatology in two months for repeat imaging. We’re not restarting your nadolol yet because of your breathing, but talk to your PCP about it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ll try to make it. I’ve missed a lot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re doing better already. Your breathing is less labored. We’ll move you to the floor tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re off BiPAP now and on room air. Your oxygen is 96%. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little wheezy, but I can talk full sentences now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re spacing out your nebulizers. We also checked your immune levels—your IgG is low, which makes sense with long-term steroids. That’s why you’re prone to CMV and other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the steroids are helping my asthma but hurting my immunity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re giving you atovaquone to prevent pneumonia while you’re on the steroid taper. You’ll stop it once the prednisone is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long is the taper?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sixty milligrams for one more day, then 40 mg for five days, 20 mg for five, then 10 mg for five. It’s important to finish it to avoid a rebound flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe it’s from the CMV gastritis. You’re on valganciclovir once daily now for three months. We’ll stop the IV pain meds. You can restart your Suboxone at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been clean for six months. I just drank because I couldn’t breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But alcohol can worsen both your liver and asthma. We’re glad you’re committed. Your pulmonologist will want to see you soon—maybe a sleep study too, for CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble sleeping. Snoring a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with asthma and obesity. The sleep team will help. You may also need allergy testing after the steroids are done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Platelets are still low, but that’s expected with cirrhosis. No signs of infection. How’s your skin? We added a steroid cream for your eczema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better. Less itchy. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well. You’ll need several follow-ups: pulmonology, sleep medicine, and liver clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. Will they call me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, pulmonology will call to schedule. The others are set. And please call your Suboxone doctor if you run low before your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go back to using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making good choices. One more thing—your asthma keeps flaring, and we don’t know why. After the taper, you may need a neck CT to check for airway collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Airway collapse? Like my throat closing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. Tracheobronchomalacia—weak airways that narrow when you breathe out. It can mimic asthma. It’s just a possibility we need to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it. I just want to breathe normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your breathing is at baseline. We’re discharging you today. Let’s go over your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your inhalers, omeprazole, and diuretics. Prednisone taper as we discussed. Valganciclovir once daily for three months. Atovaquone daily until the steroids are done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Suboxone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, restart today. Call your provider if you need more before your appointment. Nadolol is on hold—check with your PCP when it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid alcohol completely. Watch for worsening breathing, fever, or severe abdominal pain. If any of those happen, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve worked hard. Keep up the progress. The nurse will give you your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointments. I want to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but I can breathe. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go. Remember your follow-ups and the prednisone schedule. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow through. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Call us if you need anything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, chronic steroid-dependent asthma, and CMV gastritis was admitted for an acute asthma exacerbation and worsening epigastric pain following a recent alcohol binge. He was treated with BiPAP, intravenous steroids, and nebulizers, with gradual improvement in respiratory status. His abdominal pain was attributed to a flare of CMV gastritis, and he was restarted on valganciclovir. Alcohol withdrawal was monitored with CIWA, though symptoms were mild. He was discharged on a prednisone taper, atovaquone for PCP prophylaxis, and continued valganciclovir. Follow-up was arranged with pulmonology, sleep medicine, and hepatology for ongoing management of asthma, possible sleep apnea, and a liver nodule noted on prior imaging. He committed to sobriety and medication adherence.
